title: Chest pain, drooling and high fever in a fully vaccinated 10-year-old

source.citation: Ferreira M, Condessa L, Roquette M, Antão R, Cardoso C, Chaves M. Haemophilus influenzae Epiglottitis: A Rare Disease Not to Be Forgotten. Cureus. 2026;18(1):e101680.

presentation.chiefComplaint: High fever, painful swallowing, chest pain and shortness of breath
presentation.hpi: A previously healthy boy with an abrupt illness: high fever, pain on swallowing, chest pain and difficulty breathing. His vaccinations are complete, including four doses of Hib vaccine, and there is no known sick contact or other exposure.
pmh: Complete vaccination schedule, including four doses of Hib conjugate vaccine

exam: Toxic-appearing and febrile, in respiratory distress
Avoids lying supine; sits with his tongue protruding and drooling
No muffled voice and no stridor

investigations.name: Blood culture
investigations.value: Non-typable Haemophilus influenzae, susceptible to ampicillin and cefotaxime

imaging.finding: Enlarged epiglottis with the classic thumbprint sign
Inflamed, edematous supraglottic structures without glottic obstruction

diagnosis.primary: Acute epiglottitis due to non-typable Haemophilus influenzae with bacteremia in a fully Hib-vaccinated child

management: Volume resuscitation for tachycardia and a capillary refill time of 3 s
High-flow oxygen, nebulized adrenaline and IV ceftriaxone in the ED
Continuous monitoring with an experienced airway team on standby; the airway stayed stable and intubation was not needed
Intermediate care unit with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring: IV ceftriaxone plus clindamycin, prednisolone and nebulized adrenaline
outcome: Progressive clinical and laboratory improvement; discharged after 7 days to complete 3 more days of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate, with a good response.
teachingPoints: Epiglottitis still occurs after Hib vaccination, caused by non-type b and non-typable H. influenzae, streptococci or S. aureus, and increasingly affects older children and adults.
The presentation can be atypical (chest pain and dyspnea without stridor or a muffled voice); toxicity, drooling, refusal to lie supine and a tripod posture are the clues.

Keep the child upright and calm with a caregiver, avoid tongue depressors, cannulation struggles and the supine position, and bring the most experienced airway team to secure the airway in a controlled setting if needed.
A lateral neck film (thumb sign) is supportive only and must not delay airway management.
Empirical therapy: a third-generation cephalosporin plus an anti-staphylococcal agent with MRSA activity (e.g., ceftriaxone plus clindamycin or vancomycin).

questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toxic appearance, high fever, odynophagia, drooling, refusal to lie down and a tripod posture indicate supraglottic obstruction; epiglottitis still occurs in Hib-vaccinated children, and stridor or a muffled voice may be absent. Tracheitis and croup present with stridor and a barking cough, and retropharyngeal abscess typically affects younger children with neck stiffness or torticollis.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate approach in the resuscitation bay?
options: Lay him supine and examine the pharynx with a tongue depressor
Send him to radiology for a contrast-enhanced CT of the neck
Keep him upright and calm, give oxygen and call senior anesthesia and ENT
Insert a supraglottic airway now to protect against obstruction
questions.explanation: With suspected epiglottitis, agitation, the supine position and pharyngeal instrumentation can precipitate complete obstruction: give oxygen in the position of comfort and have the most experienced airway operators ready, with a surgical airway as backup (APLS approach to upper-airway obstruction). Supraglottic devices are avoided, and imaging must not delay airway control.

questions.q: Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.extra: Lateral neck radiograph: thumbprint sign. Indirect laryngoscopy: supraglottic edema without glottic obstruction. Blood cultures pending.
questions.explanation: Empirical cover must include H. influenzae (including beta-lactamase producers), S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes and S. aureus: a third-generation cephalosporin plus an anti-staphylococcal agent with MRSA activity (clindamycin or vancomycin, per local resistance). Ampicillin alone misses beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae and S. aureus; oral therapy is inappropriate for a threatened airway.

questions.q: Why did four doses of Hib vaccine not prevent this infection?
options: Hib protection wanes completely by school age
Hib vaccine prevents carriage but not invasive disease
A booster dose is required at 10 years of age
The conjugate vaccine targets only the type b capsule
questions.explanation: Hib conjugate vaccines are directed against the type b capsular polysaccharide, so non-typable (unencapsulated) strains and other serotypes are not covered; they now cause a growing share of invasive H. influenzae disease, including epiglottitis in vaccinated children. Hib vaccine protects against invasive disease and reduces carriage, and no booster at 10 years is recommended.

evidence.quote: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with an acute onset of high fever, odynophagia, chest pain, and dyspnea.
His clinical history revealed a complete vaccination schedule, including four doses of the Hib vaccine, and no known epidemiological context.
This patient was in respiratory distress, febrile, and had a toxic appearance.
He would avoid the supine position while sticking his tongue out and drooling
although oxygen saturation was >96% and lung sounds were clear to auscultation bilaterally
Given a heart rate of 130 bpm and a capillary refill time of three seconds, volume resuscitation was initiated
volume resuscitation was initiated, together with high-flow oxygen therapy, nebulized adrenaline, and ceftriaxone
Physical examination also revealed red and enlarged tonsils.
the patient's main complaints upon admission were acute chest pain and shortness of breath. He did not exhibit a muffled voice or stridor.
suspicion of epiglottitis arose due to the combination of high fever, septic appearance, respiratory distress, sore throat, and tripod positioning
leukocytosis (21,200/μL), neutrophilia (18,630/μL), elevated C-reactive protein (32.76 mg/dL), and procalcitonin (0.76 ng/mL)
Haemoglobin (g/dL) | 13.6 | 11.5-15.5
The chest radiograph was unremarkable; however, the lateral neck radiograph showed an enlarged epiglottis, creating the classic 'thumbprint' sign
the otorhinolaryngologist was able to perform indirect laryngoscopy, revealing inflammation and edema of supraglottic structures without glottic obstruction
Isolation of non-typable H. influenzae in blood culture confirmed the diagnosis.
H. infuenzae: Sensitivity to ampicillin and cefotaxime
this case of non-typable H. influenzae epiglottitis in a fully vaccinated 10-year-old boy
because the airway remained stable with no signs of deterioration, emergent intubation was not required
Continuous monitoring was ensured, and an experienced airway management team was placed on standby.
admitted into an intermediate care unit under continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring, the patient received IV ceftriaxone, clindamycin, prednisolone, and nebulized adrenaline

Following progressive clinical and laboratory improvement, the patient was discharged after seven days and completed three additional days of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate with a good response to treatment.
